title: The Way of Perfection
hookLine: Teresa's three foundations: love, detachment, humility

cards: A handful of nuns in a small, poor convent in Ávila have a request for the woman who founded it: teach us to pray.
She is Teresa, the Spanish Carmelite you first met on day twenty, who had pushed to start a house where the sisters could live the old Rule more strictly. She agrees, and she writes them a book.
But when they open it, expecting to go straight to the prayers, she makes them wait. Before a single word on how to pray, she talks about how to live.

teach.b: Teresa calls the book The Way of Perfection, and she lays down three foundations. First, love for one another.
Not a warm feeling about the community in general, but the daily kind: patience with the sister who annoys you, real concern when someone is sick.
She warns against two failures: too little love, and a clingy love that plays favorites. It echoes John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "That you love one another, as I have loved you."

teach.h: SECOND: NOT BEING OWNED BY THINGS.
teach.b: Second, detachment from created things. Not hating the world; not being owned by it, by comfort, by possessions, even by your own reputation.
Third, humility. And here she does something unexpected. She lists humility last, but calls it the most important of the three, because it holds the others together.

Why build prayer on these? Because, for Teresa, prayer isn't a technique you can run while the rest of life goes on unchanged. A person who resents everyone at breakfast will bring that resentment into the chapel.
So she starts lower, in the kitchen and the hallway.
Only then does the book turn to prayer, and when it does, it walks slowly through the Our Father, the prayer the sisters already knew by heart.

teach.h: THAT YOU LOVE ONE ANOTHER, AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.
teach.b: Her order of things works outside a convent too. For Teresa, an hour of prayer is shaped by the hours around it: how you spoke to people, what you clung to, whether you needed to win.

how: Carmelite nuns, and others who learn prayer from Teresa, read The Way of Perfection as a guide to community life and to prayer, including its slow commentary on the Our Father.

games.q: what does “the way of perfection” mean?
o: Teresa's book: love, detachment, humility, then prayer
Teresa's own story of her visions and her raptures
a rulebook for nuns on how to live without fault

p: patience with the sister who annoys you
last on the list, chief of all

s: Teresa's book jumps straight into prayer methods
she starts with how to live: love, detachment and humility come first.
Teresa calls humility the most important of the three
it comes last in her list, but she says it holds the others together.
detachment, for Teresa, means hating the world
it means not being owned by comfort, things, or even your own reputation.

games.q: you're Teresa. your sisters ask you to teach them to pray. where do you begin the book?
o: with a method for breathing and posture.
with how to live together: love, detachment, humility.
with your most dramatic experiences in prayer.
games.why: she lays three foundations first, and only then turns to prayer, walking slowly through the Our Father.

practice: Choose one of the three: a patient, kind thing for someone you'll see, one thing you hold too tightly and can loosen a little, or one small credit you could let someone else have. Just one.
If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, simply hold the choice quietly for a while.

wordCard.voice: The Way of Perfection. Teresa's book for her sisters: love, detachment, humility first, then prayer. This week moved from the Jesuits to Elijah's mountain, the Rule, the scapular, and now Teresa. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish, the title Teresa's book goes by: the way, or road, of perfection.

carryVoice: Your line: three foundations. Love, detachment and humility, laid before any talk of prayer. That's today, done.
